query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Transient liquid‐phase sintering using a Ni‐based low‐melting additive forms a graded interfacial layer between W and Cu, overcoming void formation.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or regions in a Cu matrix produced by conventional powder processing that typically suffer from phase separation and interfacial voids.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor (<5 wt%) addition of a Ni-rich Cu–Ni alloy that forms a transient liquid eutectic at around 900 °C at the W/Cu interfaces.
generation.conditions: Sinter in an inert atmosphere using controlled heating cycles that activate transient melting at the interfaces without fully liquefying the parent metals; maintain a brief dwell time so that the liquid phase is confined to the interfacial region.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanoscale graded interfacial layer that forms upon solidification of the transient liquid phase, ensuring a smooth chemical transition between W and Cu.
generation.mechanism: The transient liquid wets the W particle surfaces and the surrounding Cu matrix, fills microvoids, and then solidifies into a coherent interlayer that minimizes sharp interfaces and reduces defect density, thereby improving thermal and mechanical bonding.
generation.predicted_outcome: A W–Cu composite exhibiting significantly enhanced interfacial bonding with a graded, void‐free interface and improved thermal transport properties and irradiation tolerance relative to composites produced without the additive.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composites manufactured without any low-melting additive, which typically display sharp, defect-prone interfaces and microstructural discontinuities.
generation.boundary: Effective as long as the sintering temperature remains below values that would cause extensive Cu evaporation or unwanted intermetallic reactions, and service conditions do not exceed the thermal stability range (~<1000 °C) of the graded interlayer.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term chemical and microstructural stability of the Ni-based interlayer under extended irradiation and thermal cycling remains to be validated through accelerated tests.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of composites under identical inert sintering conditions—one with the Ni-based additive and one without. Subject the samples to detailed microstructural analysis and accelerated thermal/irradiation cycling.
measurements: SEM/TEM imaging of the interfacial region
Mechanical testing post-irradiation and thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the additive-containing composites do not demonstrate a graded, void-free interface with statistically significant improvements in thermal and mechanical performance compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. Both (as-sintered) alloys were irradiated with Ar+ (150 keV) with a fluence of 2.4 × 1020 at/m2, as well as He+ (10 keV) and D+ (5 keV) both with a fluence of 5 × 1021 at/m2. Th

Re was also avoided in order to prevent the formation of irradiation-induced embrittling precipitates, . Titanium (Ti) and vanadium (V), representing a broader definition of refractory metals, were also selected. Ti plays a significant role in improving the sintered density,  through rapid and significant interdiffusion, mass transport through the interfaces, and rearrangements of particles, , , whereas V aids in improving the strength and hardness of refractory HEAs. Another refractory metal, chromium (Cr), was also chosen for use considering its ability to impart passivation. The low neutron activation properties of W, Ta, Ti, V and Cr also favor their selection for the development of materials for potential fusion plasma facing applications. The synthesis technique was selected considering its influence on the properties of the engineering materials; e.g., alloys undergo segregation when prepared by melting, and embrittlement and porosity are attributes of conventional sintering, whereas the low thickness of the final product is a limit of the physical vapor deposition (PVD) approach. This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al0.3NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments.
